title: He Towered Above Us
subtitle: Nolan Ryan Williams, M.D. looms large, then and now.
body_html:
This is a screenshot from Nolan’s recent TED Talk, where he presented a story about the healing power of ibogaine, with its protective friend, magnesium:

He was—physically—a giant. I’m all of 5’8”, myself. I’m not tall. I don’t tower over almost anyone, and talking to Nolan, when standing up, always involved craning my neck. He recently died by suicide, as many of my readers are aware. Here's the obituary in The Times. This is an article about some of Nolan's work, and in part, it's how I am processing my feelings of grief and loss.

I've spent some time recently talking to people who knew him, including people who grew up with him, his mother, his brother, friends, and loved ones. Here's some of what I learned.

Nolan grew up in the Low Country of South Carolina. This is not a part of the same universe in which I grew up, as far as I can tell. It's a little bit like that picture, where you have another human for comparison, which can help you understand how tall Nolan was. It's much taller than the other guy; it's uncomfortably taller than the other guy.

Nolan had a younger brother, Kyle Williams, whom I've known for a few years now. One of the precious few bright spots in the loss of a friend is that the community around that person comes together, and it's especially true with Nolan. I've learned a lot about what he was like as a kid. This is a big brother, quite literally a big brother, who protected. He protected Kyle when they were kids, never bullied him. By his mother’s own admission, Ann was ready to discipline her children if they stepped out of line. Nolan didn't need it. Even as a young kid, he was self-disciplined in a way that most are not. His brother will freely admit that he wasn't like Nolan—he got into trouble, like most kids. Nolan didn't seem to need the discipline most of us do; he was disciplined already, inside himself.

One of the ways in which he was disciplined—his friends will laugh at this—was that every once in a while, he would say no to yet another scientific obligation. I was working on a series of papers last year, eventually published in the American Journal of Therapeutics, as a reference for primary care Doctors on the topic of psychedelic medicines. He helped us on that series of articles, but eventually declined to become co-Author, while in introducing us to a member of his colleagues who did eventually serve as co-authors on that series of publications. This is all while his now seminal paper on the combination of Ibogaine and magnesium was “in the oven” with reviewers at a very prestigious journal.

Even though he didn't eventually serve as a co-author on our series of publications, he did notice the authors on the team. Subsequently, he became close with both Dr. Burton Tabaac, my dear friend and collaborator, and Dr. Kenneth Sinozuka, who ended up in Nolan’s academic lab at Stamford.

Recently, that group has had a follow-up publication:

Mystical experiences during magnesium-Ibogaine are associated with improvements in PTSD symptoms in veterans

Frequent readers of this newsletter will recognize that I am a skeptic, re: psychedelic exceptionalism. I don't take it for granted that mystical experiences matter, or that so-called integration therapy is either necessary or effective. None of which is to say I don't think these things might matter, but, similar to Nolan, I believe they are empirical questions we need to ask and answer before we can have strong opinions about their importance.

In this publication, we have more data to support one pillar of the difference between psychic medicines and traditional medicines for trauma: in his cohort given magnesium-Ibogaine, the data support the strength of the mystical experience as correlated with the degree of improvement demonstrated:

That's one hell of a correlation coefficient! The paper continues:

In summary, higher intensity of mystical experiences was associated with greater reductions in PTSD severity at both immediate-post and 1-month post-treatment.

Trauma can be healed. The strength of the mystical experience with this compound is predictive of treatment outcome.

However, you have to get treatment that will heal the trauma, especially when it's severe; it's not gonna work itself out on its own reliably. For people to receive that treatment, it must be covered, accessible, and available in a private setting.

For people experiencing trauma, which is many of us, that traumatic experience comes with shame, and the bell jar of that traumatic experience can make it impossible to see how much that shame doesn't need to fall upon your own shoulders. Trauma distorts our understanding of the world, and even if we know a treatment might be available, the potency of the guilt, shame, fear, and worry that clouds our minds as a result of our experiences can make it difficult to want to get a treatment that other people could find out about. It's not that trauma, depression, or other maladies of the mind should be shameful; it's that depressed and traumatized minds find things that aren't inherently shameful to be so. That's a symptom of the disorder. This serves as a barrier to getting the treatments that could heal us. So we don't have to agree with shame. Still, we do have to understand that it exists, and that privacy enhances the ability of people’s willingness, in the grip of suffering, to access healing that can deliver them in the end.

Accessible treatment is private. Private treatment is more accessible, more powerful, and more life-saving, saving more lives. Nolan, to be clear, did not get this or any of his other innovations for himself before his death. The system of care around these things failed him, not his science. It is worth calling out, both for his memory and for the hope for those still struggling or with struggles yet to come.

Let's keep that in mind as we move forward, together, to better treatments for more individuals. Thank you, Nolan, for lighting the way.
